title: Tenses Quiz 2
description: Use have or has with the past participle, and choose between since, for, yet and already.
instructions: Read each question carefully, then check your answer.
Every question has a trap. Read every word.

questions.question: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: A period that started in the past and continues uses the present perfect with since and a point in time. Watch out: for needs a length of time, such as for five years, not a year date.

questions.question: Which sentence is correct?
options: She has been in Paris since three years.
She has been in Paris for three years.
She is in Paris for three years.
She is in Paris since three years.
questions.explanation: For + length of time, with the present perfect. Watch out: since needs a starting point, so since three years is wrong.

questions.question: {{1}} you ever {{2}} (see) a lion?
questions.explanation: Experience questions use have + past participle. Watch out: the past participle of see is seen, not saw.

questions.question: He {{1}} his homework yet. (not finish)
questions.explanation: The negative is has not + past participle, and yet goes at the end. Watch out: with he the helper is has, not have.

questions.question: 'I have seen him yesterday' is correct.
questions.explanation: Yesterday is a finished time, so the past simple is needed: I saw him yesterday. Watch out: a finished time word never goes with the present perfect.

questions.question: Complete: 'She has ___ arrived. She is here now.'
questions.explanation: Just fits the present perfect and shows a very recent action. Watch out: the other words are finished times and need the past simple.

questions.question: 'Tom has gone to the market.' This means Tom...
options: is still away at the market
questions.explanation: Has gone means he went and is not back. Watch out: has been means he went and came back.

questions.question: Complete the table with the past participle.
questions.explanation: Many verbs have three different forms. Watch out: written has a double t, and gone is not went.

questions.question: Match each word with its use.
right: a point in time, such as Monday
a length of time, such as two hours
questions.explanation: Each word has its own place. Watch out: since and for are often mixed up.

questions.question: Put the words in the correct order.
questions.explanation: The adverb never goes between have and the past participle.

questions.question: Correct the mistake: She has went home.
questions.explanation: The past participle of go is gone. Watch out: went is the past simple form and cannot follow has.

questions.question: Which tense is 'I have been waiting for an hour'?
questions.explanation: Have + been + -ing is the present perfect continuous. Watch out: it stresses the length of the action.
